The four grand and ſolemn Bardic days are, of ancient uſage, the tvvo equinoxes, and the tvvo ſolſtices; the nevv and full moons are alſo, ſubordinately, ſolemn Bardic days: […]

s.d: (figuratively) The circumstance of a twenty-four hour time period having the day and night of equal length.
x: [D]oe but ſee his vice, / Tis to his vertue, a iuſt equinox, / The one as long as th'other: […]

s.d: One of the two points in space where the apparent path of the Sun intersects with the equatorial plane of the Earth.
(obsolete, rare) A gale (“very strong wind”) once thought to occur more frequently around the time of an equinox (sense 1), now known to be a misconception; an equinoctial gale.
x: The paſſage yet vvas good, the vvind, 'tis true, / VVas ſomevvhat high, but that vvas nothing nevv, / Nor more than uſual Equinoxes blevv.
The Equinox drove the sand into their faces or round their legs, as they dived among the sheep-haunted hollows.

s.d: (obsolete) A celestial equator (“great circle on the celestial sphere, coincident with the plane of the Earth's equator (the equatorial plane)”); also, the Earth's equator.

equip.e:
From French équiper (“to supply, fit out”), originally said of a ship, Old French esquiper (“to embark”); of Germanic origin, most probably from Old Norse skipa (“to man (a ship)”), from Proto-Germanic *skipōną (“to ship, sail, embark”).
Compare with Middle High German schipfen, German schiffern, Icelandic skipa, Old English scipian. Doublet of ship.

s.d: provide with (something) usually for a specific purpose
x: The expedition was equipped with proper clothing, food, and other necessities

s.d: provide with abilities or understanding
x: She was never equipped to be a dancer

s.d: To supply with something necessary in order to carry out a specific action or task; to provide with (e.g. weapons, provisions, munitions, rigging).
x:
1698-1699, Edmund Ludlow, Memoirs
Gave orders for equipping a considerable fleet.
A semicircular plate, with the numbers in multiples of five up to thirty miles an hour, is equipped with a pointer, which indicates accurately the speed of the car.

s.d: To dress up; to array; to clothe.
x: The country are led astray in following the town, and equipped in a ridiculous habit, when they fancy themselves in the height of the mode.

s.d: To prepare (someone) with a skill.
x: I'm sorry, but I don't feel equipped to answer that kinda question yet.
it is no more than proper that you should equip us with a vessel in which to pursue the journey which you interrupted

s.d: To equip oneself with (an item); to bring (equipment) into active use.
x: Take it down from a distance with a magic spell, or equip your sword and attack it at close range.

equipage.e: From Middle French equippage, from equipper. The "carriage" sense may be influenced by Latin equus (“horse”).

s.d: equipment and supplies of a military force
a vehicle with wheels drawn by one or more horses
(uncountable) Equipment or supplies, especially military ones.
x: Araminta, come I'll talk ſeriouſly to you now, could you but ſee vvith my Eyes the buffoonry of one Scene of Addreſs, a Lover, ſet out with all his Equipage and Appurtenances; […]

s.d: (uncountable) A type of horse-drawn carriage.
(uncountable) The carriage together with attendants; a retinue.
x: Miserable and desponding he returned to his home; while Oriana, in again taking leave of her family, was borne back in her aunt's equipage to the splendours of the Park.

s.d: (obsolete, uncountable) Military dress; uniform, armour, etc.
x: Loe-heere a description, much resembling the equipage of a compleat French-man at armes, with all his bards.

s.d: (obsolete) To furnish with an equipage.

equipment.e: From equip + -ment, or from French équipement.

s.d: an instrumentality needed for an undertaking or to perform a service
(uncountable) The act of equipping, or the state of being equipped, as for a voyage or expedition.
x: The equipment of the fleet was therefore hastened by de Witt ; in hopes that , by striking at first a successful blow , he might inspire courage into the dismayed States

s.d: (uncountable) Any items used in equipping something or someone, for example things needed for an expedition or voyage.
x: We need more gardening equipment if we want to properly landscape our yard, not just a rake and some gloves.
The sports shop sells different kits of famous clubs, and equipment from all kind of sports.

s.d: (humorous, slang, uncountable) The male genitalia.
loss of military equipment
a cessation of normal operation
x: there was a power breakdown

Etymology tree
Proto-Italic *aikʷos?
Old Latin aiquos
Latin aequus

From equi- + poise.

s.d: equality of distribution
(uncountable) A state of balance; equilibrium.
x: Government was unnerved, confounded, and in a manner suspended. Its equipoise was totally gone.
“An easy evasion”, retorted the excited bride, who had lost her mental equipoise.

s.d: (uncountable) A counterbalance.
x: Perhaps that quality which existed, in spite of the equipoise against it, in Sir Howard, was fidelity in friendship.
The cone's not fixed, it's hung by a chain from a lever, and balanced by an equipoise.

s.d: To act or make to act as an equipoise.
To cause to be or stay in equipoise.
lacking lateral dominance; being neither right-handed nor left-handed
having equal strength or efficacy
Of two sets, having a bijection with one another.
provided or fitted out with what is necessary or useful or appropriate
x: a well equipped playground
a ship equipped with every mechanical aid to navigation

s.d: provided with whatever is necessary for a purpose (as furniture or equipment or authority)
x: a furnished apartment
a completely furnished toolbox

s.d: prepared with proper equipment
x: equipped for service in the Arctic

s.d: carrying weapons
Having the equipment, resources, and skills one needs; prepared.
x: Hence, the delivery of animal health services in Cameroon faces a peculiar paradox: those who are most qualified and most equipped to deliver services are not the ones delivering them.
You don't seem very equipped for the cellars.

s.d: the act of equipping with weapons in preparation for war
equipment
x: He cannot afford to be indifferent to social habits of man, the pattern of life, individual likes and dislikes of the dwellers, household furnishings and equippings.

Having equal probability, such as any number from 1 to 6 being the equiprobable outcome of the fair toss of fair dice.
x: The random number generator is designed to generate random numbers with an equiprobable law of distribution with the limits +1 to -1.

s.d: provided or fitted out with what is necessary or useful or appropriate
x: a well equipped playground
a ship equipped with every mechanical aid to navigation

equitable.e: From French équitable, from Old French, from equité (“equity”).

s.d: fair to all parties as dictated by reason and conscience
x: equitable treatment of all citizens
an equitable distribution of gifts among the children

s.d: Marked by or having equity.
Fair, just, or impartial.
x: I may justly require you to produce that argument; nor have you any pretence to refuse so equitable a demand.
Security can be obtained but by defined rights, and these can be ensured only by equitable laws.

s.d: Relating to the general principles of justice that correct or supplement the provisions of the law; relating to equity or courts of equity.

s.d: in an equitable manner
x: the inheritance was equitably divided among the sisters

s.d: the sport of sitting on the back of a horse while controlling its movements
(uncountable) The art, practice or act of horseriding.

equity.e: From Middle English equitee, equytee, from Old French equité, from Latin aequitās (“uniformity; impartiality; fairness”).

s.d: the difference between the market value of a property and the claims held against it
the ownership interest of shareholders in a corporation
conformity with rules or standards
x: the judge recognized the fairness of my claim

s.d: (uncountable) Fairness, impartiality, or justice as determined in light of "natural law" or "natural right".
x: “One of the staff said, ‘That’s fine, Delia. But what do wolves have to do with equity, justice and inclusion?’" Ms. Malone said.

s.d: (uncountable) Various related senses originating with the Court of Chancery in late Medieval England: The power of a court of law having extra-statutory discretion, to decide legal matters and to provide legal relief apart from, though not in violation of, the prevailing legal code; in some cases, a court "sitting in equity" may provide relief to a complainant should the code be found either inapplicable or insufficient to do so.
x:
1800, Lloyd Kenyon, 1st Baron Kenyon in Mayor, &c. of Southampton v. Graves (1800), 8 T. R. 592.
A Court of equity knows its own province.
A Court of equity interposes only according to conscience.

s.d: (uncountable) Various related senses originating with the Court of Chancery in late Medieval England: A right which accrues to a party in a transaction because of the nature of the transaction itself, and which is exercisable upon a change of circumstances or conditions; in other words, an equitable claim.
x: ...the mortgagor retains ‘equitable title’ or the ‘equity of redemption’….The equity of redemption permits the mortgagor to regain legal title to the mortgaged property upon satisfying the conditions of the mortgage...

The wife's equity does not, according to the adjudged cases, attach, except upon that part of her personal property in action which the husband cannot acquire without the assistance of a court of equity

s.d: (uncountable) Various related senses originating with the Court of Chancery in late Medieval England: The body of law which was developed in the English Court of Chancery, which Court had extra-statutory discretion, and is now administered alongside the common law of Britain.
(uncountable) Various senses related to net value: Value of property minus liens or other encumbrances.
x: I have a lot of equity in my house.

s.d: (uncountable) Various senses related to net value: Ownership, especially in terms of net monetary value of some business.
(uncountable) Various senses related to net value: Ownership interest in a company as determined by subtracting liabilities from assets.
(uncountable) Various senses related to net value: A player's expected share of the pot.
(uncountable) Equality
x: What steps the Government are taking to help ensure equity of opportunity for people from low-income families.

s.d: a loan secured by equity value in the borrower's home

equivalence.e: From French équivalence, from Medieval Latin aequivalentia.

s.d: a state of being essentially equal or equivalent; equally balanced
x: on a par with the best

s.d: essential equality and interchangeability
qualities that are comparable
x: no comparison between the two books
beyond compare

s.d: (uncountable) The condition of being equivalent or essentially equal: the status of being interchangeable.
x: His answer and yours share equivalence.
Cow's milk and soy milk have a lot of differences, but their equivalence is sufficient for this recipe.

s.d: (uncountable) The relationship between two propositions that are either both true or both false.
An equivalence relation; ≡; ~.
(uncountable) A Boolean operation that is TRUE when both input variables are TRUE or both input variables are FALSE, but otherwise FALSE; the XNOR function.
(uncountable) A number in intersection theory. A positive-dimensional variety sometimes behaves formally as if it were a finite number of points; this number is its equivalence.
(uncountable) The quantity of the combining power of an atom, expressed in hydrogen units; the number of hydrogen atoms can combine with, or be exchanged for; valency.
(uncountable) The state of two notes being separated by one octave or the similarity of two such notes.
(uncountable) The degree to which a term or text in one language is semantically similar to its translated counterpart.
x: Equivalence is important, but when translating poetry, you need to get across the feel and the emotion more than the exact semantic meaning.

s.d: (uncountable) The principle that one long syllable is equal to two short ones.
To be equivalent or equal to; to counterbalance.
x: […] whether the transgression of Eve seducing, did not exceed that of Adam seduced, or whether the resistibility of his reason did not equivalence the facility of her seduction, we shall referre it unto the Schoolman.

equivalent.e:
From Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”). By surface analysis, equi- + -valent.
Mostly displaced native Middle English efenmete.

s.d: a person or thing equal to another in value or measure or force or effect or significance etc
x: send two dollars or the equivalent in stamps

s.d: the atomic weight of an element that has the same combining capacity as a given weight of another element; the standard is 8 for oxygen
Anything that is virtually equal to something else, or has the same value, force, etc.
x: He's the Italian equivalent of a district attorney.
He owned that, if the Test Act were repealed, the Protestants were entitled to an equivalent, and went so far as to suggest several equivalents.

s.d: An equivalent weight.
To make equivalent to; to equal.
being essentially equal to something
x: a wish that was equivalent to a command
his statement was tantamount to an admission of guilt

s.d: Similar or identical in value, meaning or effect; virtually equal.
x: To burn calories, a thirty-minute jog is equivalent to a couple of hamburgers.
For now to serve and to minister, servile and ministerial, are terms equivalent.

s.d: Of two sets, having a one-to-one correspondence.
x: All enumerable sets are equivalent to each other, but not to any finite set.
Equivalent sets should, by rights, have the same "number" of elements. For this reason we sometimes say that equivalent sets have the same cardinality.

s.d: Relating to the corresponding elements of an equivalence relation.

Of two categories, (informally) such that one is essentially a relabeling of the other; (formally) related by a pair of functors such the composition of the one with the other is naturally isomorphic to the identity functor.
Having the equal ability to combine.
Of a map, equal-area.
Equal in measure but not admitting of superposition; applied to magnitudes.
x: A square may be equivalent to a triangle.

s.d: the atomic weight of an element that has the same combining capacity as a given weight of another element; the standard is 8 for oxygen
The atomic weight of an element or radical divided by its valence; the molecular weight of a compound divided by its combining power in a specific reaction.
x: The equivalent weight of an element or compound is that weight equivalent in reactive power to one atomic weight of hydrogen.

s.d: two words that can be interchanged in a context are said to be synonymous relative to that context

the average number of binary digits needed to express one radix digit in a numeration system that is not binary; on the average a number that can be expressed in N decimal digits takes 3.3N binary digits

s.d: To render equivocal or ambiguous.

falsification by means of vague or ambiguous language
